title: ABRAHAM BOWED BEFORE THE HITTITES—BUT THE REAL REASON WILL CHANGE HOW YOU SEE FAITH, GRIEF, AND GOD’S PROMISES
paragraphs: ABRAHAM BOWED BEFORE THE HITTITES—BUT THE REAL REASON WILL CHANGE HOW YOU SEE FAITH, GRIEF, AND GOD’S PROMISES

He was promised an entire land by God. Yet when his wife died, he had to negotiate with strangers just to bury her. Why would the father of faith bow before people who did not share his covenant? The answer reveals something astonishing about humility, dignity, the cost of faith, and the Savior who would one day turn a burial place into a testimony of resurrection.
There is a kind of pain that nobody sees.
The kind that makes you sit quietly on the edge of your bed, staring at nothing, because the life you thought you would have is no longer the life you are living.
You prayed.
You believed.
You held on to promises from God when everything around you seemed to contradict them.
And then something happened that made you wonder whether you had misunderstood the promise all along.
A marriage ended. A loved one died. A door closed. A diagnosis changed everything. The years passed, and what God had promised still seemed painfully far away.
You know what makes that kind of suffering especially difficult?
Sometimes you are grieving while still having to negotiate with a world that does not understand your grief.
You have to make arrangements. Sign documents. Discuss money. Speak politely. Answer questions. Continue functioning when your heart is barely holding together.
And somewhere in the middle of it all, you whisper something you are almost afraid to say aloud.
“Lord, I thought You promised.”
Now imagine Abraham.
The man God had called out of his homeland.
The man who had heard the voice of the Almighty.
The man who had been promised descendants as numerous as the stars and a land that would belong to his offspring.
Now picture him standing before the Hittites.
Not with an army.
Not with a royal crown.
Not demanding what God had promised.
But bowing.
Twice.
And behind that moment of humility was a heartbreak so personal that it could have broken a lesser man.
His wife was dead.
Sarah.
The woman who had traveled with him into the unknown.
The woman who had endured years of barrenness, uncertainty, waiting, and disappointment.
The woman who had laughed when the promise of a son seemed humanly impossible.
The woman who had finally held Isaac in her arms.
Sarah was gone.
And Abraham, the man who believed God, was trying to find somewhere to bury her.
That is where Genesis 23 takes us.
And what happens next is far more profound than an ancient real-estate transaction.
Genesis 23:2 tells us that Sarah died in Kiriath-arba, which is Hebron, in the land of Canaan.
Then Scripture says:
“And Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her.” (Genesis 23:2, KJV)
Read that slowly.
Abraham wept.
The father of faith cried.
The man who had trusted God through impossible circumstances was not immune to heartbreak.
His faith did not make him emotionless.
His covenant with God did not make him incapable of sorrow.
He had believed the promises of God, but he still felt the crushing weight of losing someone he loved.
Some Christians have been taught, directly or indirectly, that strong faith means hiding grief.
That if you really trust God, you should stop crying.
That tears somehow reveal a lack of spiritual maturity.
But Genesis refuses to give us that picture.
Abraham mourned.
And centuries later, standing before the tomb of Lazarus, Jesus Himself wept (John 11:35).
Do you see it?
The Bible does not present grief as the opposite of faith.
Faith can be present in the same heart that is breaking.
You can believe in the resurrection and still miss someone terribly.
You can trust God's character and still struggle to understand His timing.
You can worship with tears running down your face.
And sometimes the holiest thing you can do is bring your broken heart honestly before the Lord instead of pretending it is not broken.
But Abraham could not remain beside Sarah's body forever.
Love now required a painful responsibility.
He needed a burial place.
And that is when Scripture introduces a sentence that changes the entire meaning of the story.
In Genesis 23:4, Abraham tells the sons of Heth:
“I am a stranger and a sojourner with you: give me a possession of a buryingplace with you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight.” (KJV)
A stranger.
A sojourner.
Let that settle into your spirit.
God had promised Abraham the land of Canaan.
Yet Abraham stood before its inhabitants and described himself as someone without a permanent landed inheritance among them.
The Hebrew is extraordinary:
גֵּר־וְתוֹשָׁב אָנֹכִי עִמָּכֶם
Ger-ve-toshav anokhi immakhem.
“I am a resident alien and a sojourner among you.”
The word גֵּר (ger) refers to a foreigner or resident outsider living among a people.
The word תּוֹשָׁב (toshav) describes someone residing or dwelling in a place without necessarily possessing the full inherited standing of its established people.
Together, the expression emphasizes Abraham's position as a resident who did not yet possess the land as his own inheritance.
And here is the tension.
He belonged to God's promise.
But he did not yet possess its fullness.
He had divine assurance.
But he still had to conduct an earthly negotiation.
He was chosen by God.
But that did not mean everyone around him had to surrender their property at his command.
This is where the story begins to confront our understanding of faith.
Because sometimes we assume that if God has promised something, we should never have to wait, ask, negotiate, or suffer for it.
We imagine faith as a shortcut around ordinary human difficulties.
But Abraham shows us something different.
A promise from God does not give us permission to abandon humility, honesty, or patience while waiting for its fulfillment.
And then comes the moment that gives this passage its astonishing depth.
Genesis 23:7 says:
“And Abraham stood up, and bowed himself to the people of the land, even to the children of Heth.” (KJV)
The Hebrew reads:
וַיָּקָם אַבְרָהָם וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ לְעַם־הָאָרֶץ לִבְנֵי־חֵת
Vayyaqom Avraham vayishtachu le'am-ha'aretz livnei-Chet.
“And Abraham rose and bowed himself to the people of the land, to the sons of Heth.”
The crucial word is וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ (vayishtachu).
It comes from the Hebrew verb shachah, meaning to bow down or prostrate oneself.
Depending on the context, this action can express worship, reverence, submission, or respectful deference.
And that distinction matters enormously.
Because someone might read this passage and ask:
Why would Abraham, the worshiper of the true God, bow before the Hittites?
Was he compromising his faith?
Was he honoring pagan gods?
Was he lowering himself before people who had no part in God's covenant?
No.
Nothing in Genesis 23 indicates that Abraham was worshiping the Hittites or their gods.
The context is a public negotiation over burial property.
His bow was a gesture of respect toward the people with whom he was dealing.
The same Hebrew verb can describe worship directed toward God or respectful bowing before human beings. Its meaning must be determined by the situation, not merely by the physical movement.
Abraham was not transferring his worship.
He was showing courtesy.
He was not surrendering his covenant.
He was acknowledging the people whose cooperation he needed.
And there is something deeply convicting here.
Abraham knew who his God was, so he did not need to prove his spiritual importance by humiliating other people.
That is a lesson the modern Church desperately needs.
We live in a world where people sometimes confuse boldness with rudeness.
Where spiritual conviction becomes an excuse for arrogance.
Where believers can become so concerned with defending their status that they forget to display the character of Christ.
But Abraham bowed.
Not because the Hittites were greater than the God who called him.
Not because God's promise had failed.
But because respect toward other people was not a betrayal of his relationship with God.
Think about how different our homes, churches, workplaces, and online conversations would become if we remembered that.
You can stand firmly for biblical truth without treating people with contempt.
You can disagree without dehumanizing.
You can refuse idolatry while showing ordinary human respect.
You can belong to God without behaving as though everyone else is beneath you.
Humility is not the absence of conviction.
Sometimes humility is the clearest evidence that conviction has reached your character.
But there is another detail that makes Abraham's behavior even more remarkable.
He was not negotiating from a position of emotional comfort.
He was grieving.
He had just lost Sarah.
He was trying to arrange her burial.
And even then, he treated the people before him with dignity.
Have you ever noticed how pain can tempt us to become harsh?
When life has wounded us, we sometimes feel entitled to wound others.
When we are exhausted, we become impatient.
When we are disappointed, we become demanding.
When we believe God has given us something, we may begin to act as though everyone else is obligated to make it happen.
But Abraham's grief did not erase his integrity.
And his confidence in God's promise did not erase his respect for other people's rights.
The Hittites responded generously.
In Genesis 23:6, they addressed him as a mighty prince among them, or more literally, נְשִׂיא אֱלֹהִים (nesi Elohim), an expression often understood as “a prince of God” or “a mighty prince.”
The exact force of the expression is debated, but the context makes their respect for Abraham unmistakable.
They offered him access to their choice burial places.
Yet Abraham had a particular location in mind.
The cave of Machpelah, belonging to Ephron son of Zohar.
And Abraham wanted to pay for it.
Not simply receive permission to use it.
Not rely upon an arrangement that could later become uncertain.
He sought a recognized possession for burial.
In Genesis 23:9, Abraham specifically asked that Ephron sell him the cave for its full price.
The Hebrew expression בְּכֶסֶף מָלֵא (bekhesef male) means “for full silver,” naturally understood here as the full purchase price.
Why does that matter?
Because Abraham was not attempting to use God's promise as a reason to take someone else's property.
God had promised the land to his descendants.
But Abraham did not turn that promise into an excuse for dishonesty or coercion.
He negotiated publicly and sought a legitimate transfer.
There is a painful kind of faith that says, “If God promised it, I should be able to seize it.”
But biblical faith is not permission to manipulate people, avoid paying what is owed, or claim ownership of something that still belongs to another person.
Abraham trusted God enough to act honorably while waiting.
And then Ephron entered the conversation.
He spoke of giving Abraham the field and cave.
But as the discussion continued, he named a price.
Four hundred shekels of silver.
Genesis 23:15 records Ephron saying:
“My lord, hearken unto me: the land is worth four hundred shekels of silver; what is that betwixt me and thee? bury therefore thy dead.” (KJV)
Four hundred shekels.
We should be careful here.
Some interpretations describe this as an outrageously inflated price or portray Ephron as deliberately dishonest.
The text itself does not provide enough comparative economic evidence to establish either conclusion with certainty.
What it does tell us is that a specific price was named and Abraham accepted it.
Genesis 23:16 says:

“And Abraham hearkened unto Ephron; and Abraham weighed to Ephron the silver, which he had named in the audience of the sons of Heth, four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant.” (KJV)
The Hebrew says:
אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שֶׁקֶל כֶּסֶף
Arba me'ot sheqel kesef.
“Four hundred shekels of silver.”
The passage describes silver weighed according to a recognized commercial standard, not modern coins stamped with denominations.
And Abraham paid.
The transaction took place before witnesses at the city gate, a recognized public setting for legal and commercial matters in the ancient Near East.
Genesis 23:17–18 carefully identifies the field, the cave, the trees, and the boundaries of the property.
This was not an incidental detail.
The narrator wants us to understand that the burial property was formally transferred.
The man who had been promised the land now possessed a small piece of it through an actual purchase.
But consider what he intended to do with that land.
He was not building a palace.
He was not establishing a military fortress.
He was not planting a vineyard to celebrate his prosperity.
He was burying his wife.
The first specifically recorded parcel of Canaan that Abraham acquired as his own was a place for the dead.
Let that sink in.
God had promised a future.
Abraham purchased a grave.
And somehow, those two realities belonged to the same story.
This is where the passage becomes almost unbearably personal.
Because some of us are living between what God has said and what we can currently see.
You know the promises of Scripture.
You know God is faithful.
You know He has not abandoned His people.
But you are still standing in front of something that looks painfully final.
A hospital bed.
A divorce decree.
A rejection letter.
A cemetery.
An empty chair at the dinner table.
A photograph of someone whose voice you would give almost anything to hear again.
And you wonder how God's goodness can coexist with this much sorrow.
Abraham's story does not give us permission to promise that every personal dream will come true or that every loss will be reversed in this lifetime.
But it does give us something stronger than wishful thinking.
It shows us that God's covenant faithfulness is not canceled by the presence of grief.
And the New Testament opens this truth even further.
Hebrews 11:9 says:
“By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country...” (KJV)
Then Hebrews 11:10 explains that Abraham looked for a city with foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
And Hebrews 11:13 speaks of faithful people who died without receiving the fullness of what had been promised, yet saw those promises from afar.
That is extraordinary.
Abraham's faith was not based upon possessing everything immediately.
It rested upon the trustworthiness of the God who had spoken.
He could purchase a burial place without concluding that God's promise had become meaningless.
He could bury Sarah without believing that death was stronger than God.
We must not pretend Genesis 23 explicitly tells us everything Abraham was thinking as he bowed or paid for the field.
It does not.
But the wider testimony of Scripture tells us that Abraham lived as a pilgrim who trusted God's future.
And that future reaches far beyond a single cave in Hebron.
Because the story of Abraham and Sarah does not end in the darkness of Machpelah.
In Genesis 25:9, Isaac and Ishmael bury Abraham in the same cave.
Later, Genesis 49:29–32 identifies the family burial place associated with Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob.
The cave became part of the continuing history of God's covenant family.
A purchased burial place remained a tangible connection to the land promised to Abraham's descendants.
But there is an even greater fulfillment to consider.
Centuries after Abraham stood before the Hittites, another Son of Abraham would enter the world.
Jesus Christ.
The promised descendant through whom the blessing to the nations would ultimately come.
Matthew 1:1 introduces Him as the son of David, the son of Abraham.
And Galatians 3:16 directs our attention to Christ as the promised offspring in whom God's redemptive purpose comes to its fulfillment.
Abraham bowed respectfully before human beings.
Jesus, the eternal Son of God, went infinitely further.
He humbled Himself.
Philippians 2:7–8 tells us that Christ took the form of a servant, became obedient unto death, even death on a cross.
Do not confuse these two acts as though they were identical.
Abraham's bow was a social gesture within a land transaction.
Christ's humiliation was the voluntary self-giving of the incarnate Son for the salvation of sinners.
But when we read Abraham's story in the light of the whole Bible, we see a beautiful harmony in the character of genuine faith.
God's people are not called to use their position as an excuse for pride.
They are called to trust, obey, and walk humbly before Him.
And Jesus reveals humility in its purest and most glorious form.
He did not merely speak kindly to those who needed Him.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He washed His disciples' feet.
He bore the shame of the cross.
He was mocked by people He had come to save.
And He gave His life for the ungodly.
Think of the contrast.
Abraham sought a burial place for the woman he loved.
Jesus entered death to rescue the people He loved.
Abraham paid silver for a cave.
Jesus redeemed His people not with silver or gold, but with His precious blood (1 Peter 1:18–19).
Abraham's purchased cave held the dead.
The tomb in which Jesus was laid could not hold Him.
And we must be precise about that glorious distinction.
Genesis 23 is not a direct prophecy that every detail of Abraham's transaction symbolizes Christ's burial.
The text does not say that.
But the unfolding biblical story moves from God's covenant promises to their fulfillment in Jesus, whose death and resurrection provide the ultimate answer to the problem of sin and death.
The burial place of Sarah reminds us that even the faithful die.
The empty tomb of Jesus announces that death does not have the final word.
And this is where the Gospel becomes intensely personal.
Because our deepest problem is not merely that life disappoints us.
It is that sin has separated humanity from the holy God who made us.
We have not simply suffered.
We have also sinned.
We have been proud when we should have been humble.
Dishonest when we should have been truthful.
Cruel when we should have been merciful.
Selfish when we should have loved.
We have demanded our rights while ignoring God's commands.
Some of us have used religious language to disguise our arrogance.
Some have confused being publicly Christian with being privately surrendered.
Some have quoted Scripture while refusing to forgive.
Some have spoken about holiness while protecting secret sins.
And some have become so accustomed to pretending that we no longer remember what honest repentance feels like.
But here is the scandal of grace.
Jesus did not come because we had made ourselves worthy.
He came because we needed a Savior.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were still sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputations.
Not after we cleaned up every failure.
Not after we became impressive enough to deserve His attention.
Christ died for us.
And because He rose again, forgiveness is not an empty religious slogan.
It is the gift of the living Savior to those who repent and believe in Him.
Maybe that is what you need to hear tonight.
Not that you are strong enough to carry everything.
Not that your tears are embarrassing.
Not that your past was harmless.
Not that God approves of everything you have done.
But that Jesus Christ is sufficient to save sinners who come to Him.
You do not need to disguise your guilt before the One who already knows the truth.
You do not need to perform spiritual confidence while your heart is trembling.
You can confess.
You can repent.
You can ask for mercy.
You can come to Christ.
And if you belong to Him, you can grieve with hope because His resurrection is the pledge of the resurrection of His people.
First Thessalonians 4:13 does not tell believers never to sorrow.
It tells us not to sorrow as those who have no hope.
That distinction is everything.
Christian hope does not erase love's pain.
It anchors that pain in the victory of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps you are reading this with a wound nobody else knows about.
Perhaps you have been disappointed with God because the answer to your prayer did not arrive when you expected.
Perhaps you have been angry because you did what you believed was right and still lost something precious.
Perhaps you are serving in church while privately wondering whether your faith is surviving.
Remember Abraham.
He stood before the Hittites without possessing the full inheritance God had promised.
He bowed respectfully.
He paid honestly.
He buried Sarah.
And the promises of God had not failed.
He did not have to possess everything to keep trusting the One who had promised.
And neither do you.
But there is another uncomfortable truth hidden in this passage.
Some of us need to learn to bow.
Not before idols.
Not before sin.
Not before spiritual manipulation.
But in humility.
We need to stop confusing our calling with superiority.
We need to apologize to the people we have wounded.
We need to conduct our business honestly.
We need to treat those who do not share our faith with dignity.
We need to stop acting as though being chosen by grace gives us permission to become arrogant.
The world does not need Christians who merely announce that they know God while displaying a character that contradicts His Word.
It needs to see lives being transformed by the Gospel.
Jesus said in Matthew 5:16 that our light should shine before others so they may see our good works and glorify our Father in heaven.
That does not mean every respectful gesture will lead someone to faith.
But it does mean our conduct matters.
Abraham's faith was not detached from the way he treated people.
Ours should not be either.
And if this passage has exposed pride, bitterness, dishonesty, or a wound you have been hiding, do not rush past that conviction.
Bring it before Christ.
Maybe your prayer needs to be simple.

“Lord Jesus, forgive me for the ways I have misrepresented You. Forgive my pride. Forgive my hidden sin. Teach me to trust You when Your promises seem distant. Teach me to grieve without surrendering hope. Make my life reflect Your humility, truth, and love. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Help me follow You faithfully. Amen.”
And if you cannot find the words for a longer prayer, begin with this:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
He is not impressed by the length of our religious performances.
He calls us to genuine faith and repentance.
There may be someone reading this who has not prayed honestly in months.
Someone who still attends worship but feels spiritually exhausted.
Someone who has stopped opening the Bible because every promise seems to remind them of what they lost.
Someone who needs to know that the Lord is not indifferent to the brokenhearted.
Psalm 34:18 tells us:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.” (KJV)
Do not mistake God's nearness for a guarantee that every circumstance will change immediately.
His presence is not a promise of an easy life.
But His grace is sufficient for His people, and His resurrection promises a future no grave can ultimately destroy.
That is why stories like this matter.
Not because we are trying to manufacture an emotional moment.
But because the Word of God reaches places that ordinary encouragement cannot reach.
Sometimes a person does not need another motivational slogan.
They need to open Genesis 23 and discover that even Abraham had to stand in a painful place while waiting for God's promise.
Sometimes they need to learn that bowing respectfully before another person is not the same as surrendering their faith.
Sometimes they need to discover that Christian humility is not weakness.
Sometimes they need to hear that the Savior who conquered the grave understands the tears we shed beside one.
And maybe that is why you should not keep this article to yourself.
Think of one person who is grieving.
One friend who has been disappointed.
One family member who is carrying silent bitterness.
One believer who has become proud and needs a loving reminder of Christ's humility.
One person who thinks their suffering means God has abandoned them.
You never know when a passage someone has overlooked for years may become the very Scripture God uses to draw them back to His Word.
And please, do not disappear without telling us what this passage awakened in your heart.
You do not have to disclose private wounds publicly. A simple prayer request is enough.
Someone else may need the encouragement of knowing that faith can survive a season of tears.
There may come a day when you need to return to it.
A day when the funeral is over, the visitors have gone home, the house is quiet, and grief feels heavier than it did before.
A day when you are tempted to confuse delay with abandonment.
A day when you need to remember that Abraham was still God's covenant servant while standing before a grave.

We want this community to be a place where biblical truth is taken seriously, where repentance is not avoided, where wounded people are treated with compassion, and where everything ultimately points to Jesus Christ.
And if this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, return to prayer, or grow in your walk with Christ, I want to invite you to consider something more personal.
Not because God will love you more if you give.
Not because you must pay to receive His grace.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Scripture teaches that those who receive spiritual instruction may share good things with those who teach (Galatians 6:6), and that believers may generously support Gospel work (Philippians 4:15–18).
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the heart of this invitation.
If you already give faithfully to your local church, please do not neglect that responsibility.
It is an additional, voluntary way to participate in this particular work if you are able and feel led to do so.
Your monthly contribution can function as a ministry offering toward the continuation and expansion of Gospel Warrior's biblical teaching, discipleship resources, and outreach.
It helps make possible more articles, more Scriptural encouragement, and more opportunities to point people to the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
It is participation in work that seeks to make Christ known.
Those free resources are part of our desire to help believers grow deeper in Scripture, prayer, holiness, and the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
You can still help.
Pray that the teaching will remain faithful to Scripture.
Encourage another believer to open the Bible.
Speak the name of Jesus with courage and compassion.
Every act of faithful service matters, even when nobody applauds.
Because this was never supposed to be about building a platform greater than the message.
It is about making much of Christ.
The One who forgives sinners.
The One who restores the repentant.
The One who receives the weary.
The One who died and rose again.
The One who is worthy of all glory.
And now, before you leave, return with me to that scene in Genesis one last time.
An old man stands before the inhabitants of the land.
His beloved wife is gone.
The future God promised has not yet arrived in its fullness.
He bows.
He negotiates.
He weighs out the silver.
He receives the field and the cave.
And then he lays Sarah to rest.
No thunder from heaven.
No dramatic miracle recorded in that chapter.
No angel appearing to explain the delay.
Just a grieving husband, an honest transaction, and a promise that remained greater than what he could see.
But the story was not over.
God would continue His covenant purposes through Isaac, Jacob, and the generations that followed.
And in the fullness of time, Jesus Christ would come.
He would bear our sins on the cross.
He would be laid in a tomb.
And on the third day, He would rise.
So when you think about Abraham bowing before the Hittites, remember what the passage actually teaches.
Humility is not the surrender of faith.
Respect is not the worship of human beings.
Grief is not proof that God has abandoned you.
And waiting does not make God's promises untrue.
Most importantly, do not leave this story merely admiring Abraham.
Look to the greater fulfillment of God's promise.
Look to Jesus.
Because Abraham's story teaches us how faith can endure while the promise is still unseen.
But Jesus Christ is the One in whom God's redemptive promises find their decisive fulfillment.
And if you are in Christ, even the grave cannot cancel the future He has secured for you.
So come to Him with your grief.
Come with your repentance.
Come with your questions.
Come with the life you never imagined you would have to live.
Trust the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
And remember this when the night becomes unbearably quiet:
Abraham could not keep Sarah from the grave, but the risen Jesus has made sure the grave will never have the final word over those who belong to Him.
